extraction_text: Yudhishthira expresses his belief in the teachings of dharma but has several questions about the rewards for various virtuous actions.

attributes.relationships: Yudhishthira seeks wisdom from his grandfather Bhishma about dharma

extraction_text: Yudhishthira asks about the rewards for: observing vows, self-restraint, studying the Vedas, controlling desires, reciting the Vedas, teaching the Vedas, refusing gifts, teaching traditional knowledge, performing caste duties, heroism, truthfulness, celibate life, respecting parents, respecting teachers, and showing compassion.

attributes.purpose: To understand the practical benefits of righteous living

extraction_text: Bhishma explains that faithfully observing one's vows leads to eternal happiness in the afterlife.
Bhishma states that self-restraint brings visible rewards in this world and the next, citing Yudhishthira's own experience with purity and ritual performance.

attributes.relationship_note: Bhishma uses Yudhishthira's own life as example

extraction_text: Bhishma explains that studying the Vedas brings prosperity in this life and eternal happiness in the next.
Bhishma describes how controlling desires leads to contentment, ability to defeat enemies, fulfillment of wishes, and attainment of heaven through austerity or valor.
Bhishma compares self-restraint to charity/sacrifice, stating that self-restraint is superior because it avoids anger that can destroy the merit of giving.

attributes.philosophical_point: Self-restraint is higher than mere charity

extraction_text: Bhishma describes thousands of invisible celestial realms where sages become deities after death, attained through self-restraint.

attributes.supernatural_element: Invisible heavenly worlds, transformation into deities

extraction_text: The text describes various types of virtuous individuals and their corresponding rewards in the afterlife.

characters: Listener (addressed as 'People's Lord', 'Hero of the Bharata clan', 'Lord of the Earth')
attributes.relationships: Teacher-student relationship between narrator and listener

extraction_text: Teachers who impart knowledge and worship Agni (fire god) with proper rituals can transcend earthly suffering and enjoy eternal happiness in Brahma's world.
Those who study Vedas diligently, teach properly, and praise their teachers gain high honor in heaven.
Kshatriyas who study diligently, perform timely sacrifices, give generously, and show bravery in war gain high honor in heaven.
Vaishyas who fulfill caste duties and give generously receive great rewards; Shudras who fulfill caste duties through patient endurance reach heaven in the next life.

Various types of heroes are described: sacrificial heroes, self-disciplined heroes, honest heroes, battlefield heroes, generous heroes, learned heroes, tolerant heroes, honest heroes, calm heroes, and others who follow various disciplines.
All these heroes attain corresponding rewards and go to different happy worlds based on their good deeds.
Truthfulness is weighed against a thousand horse sacrifices and found to be heavier; truth is declared the highest dharma.
Truth sustains the sun's heat, fire's light, and wind's movement; everything in the world is based on truth.
Sages take truth as their duty, source of strength, and basis for oaths; truthful people enjoy happiness in heaven.
The narrator concludes by stating they will explain the merits of purity, and that those who maintain purity from birth to death can achieve any goal.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about the most important rules for donating cows.
Bhishma explains that there is no higher merit than donating cows, and that properly donating a cow can immediately save the donor's entire family.
Bhishma recounts that in ancient times, someone brought cows before King Mandhata, who became confused and sought instruction from Brihaspati.

attributes.relationship: King seeks guidance from divine sage

extraction_text: Brihaspati instructs Mandhata on the proper procedure for cow donation, including purification rituals, selecting auspicious time, choosing specific cows (Rohini type), and reciting mantras.
The donor must spend the night in the cowshed with the cows, reciting mantras that declare the cow as mother and bull as father, seeking earthly happiness and heavenly afterlife.

attributes.spiritual_element: Soul connection with cows to remove past sins

extraction_text: The next morning at sunrise, the donor gives a cow along with a bull and calf to a Brahmin, praising cows for their triple characteristics as sources of strength, wisdom, immortality, and prosperity.
The donor recites verses wishing for blessings from cattle to guide him to heaven, provide food and shelter, and grant all unmentioned benefits.
The donor states that after giving, he will have nothing left, and through his actions, his body is liberated. He compares the blessings from cattle to those from the Sarasvati River.
The donor declares that he has become like the cattle and by giving them, he gives himself. The recipient then responds, stating the cattle are now his and shine like the moon in the sky.

attributes.relationship_change: Transfer of ownership from donor to recipient

extraction_text: Instructions are given: the donor should recite the first part of the verses according to rules, and the recipient, a learned twice-born, should respond with the second part while accepting.
If a donor has no cattle to give, he can substitute with other useful items like clothes or gold, declaring it as a gift of cattle and naming it as 'Udasya cow', 'Bhrithavya cow', or 'Vishnavi cow'.

attributes.action: Substitution of donation with alternative items

extraction_text: The type of cattle should be specified during donation. As a result, the donor can go to heaven for varying durations: 26,000, 8,000, or 20,000 years.

attributes.action: Specification of cattle type and heavenly reward

extraction_text: The merit from donating cattle or substitutes varies by the item given. The donor's merit is secured when the recipient takes the eighth step home.

attributes.action: Acquisition of merit based on donation
attributes.supernatural_elements: Merit transfer linked to recipient's actions

extraction_text: Benefits are described: donating cattle makes one virtuous, donating substitutes frees one from fear, donating gold prevents suffering from desires, leading to becoming learned, a follower of Vishnu, and entering the world of the moon god.

attributes.action: Listing of spiritual benefits from donations
attributes.supernatural_elements: Transformation into virtuous, fearless, and enlightened states; entry into divine realms

extraction_text: After donating cattle, the donor should observe a three-day cattle vow, live with cattle for a day, and from the eighth lunar day (Kamya), live for three days on milk, dung, and urine of cattle.

Merits are compared: donating a bull equals the merit of observing Vedic vows, donating a pair equals learning the Vedas, and donating after a sacrifice allows access to superior worlds, unlike those ignorant of rules.

attributes.action: Comparison of donation merits to other spiritual acts
attributes.supernatural_elements: Access to superior worlds based on knowledge and ritual

extraction_text: Donating a single milch cow yields merit equal to giving all worldly desires, and donating a bull surpasses the merit of extensive offerings to gods and ancestors.

attributes.action: Highlighting supreme merit of specific donations

extraction_text: Bhishma advises Yudhishthira on rules for donating cows, specifying who should not be taught these rules.

attributes.details: Rules should not be taught to: non-students, rule-breakers, those lacking faith, and those who misinterpret scriptures.

extraction_text: Bhishma warns against giving donations to evil people without faith, as it brings misfortune.

attributes.details: Many people have pure faith, but there are also evil people like Rakshasas. Donating to the faithless causes misfortune.

extraction_text: Bhishma lists kings who followed Brihaspati's teachings on cow donation and attained eternal happiness.

attributes.details: Kings include: Ushinara, Vishvakasena, Nriga, Bhagiratha, Mandhata, Muchukunda, Prithushravas, Nala, Somaka, Pururavas, Bharata, Rama, and Dilipa.

extraction_text: Bhishma instructs Yudhishthira to remember Brihaspati's teachings and donate cows to excellent Brahmins after gaining the Kuru kingdom.

attributes.details: Yudhishthira should donate auspicious cows to top Brahmins with a happy heart after securing the throne.

extraction_text: Yudhishthira learns the proper rules from Bhishma and begins practicing cow donation rigorously.

attributes.details: He ties up his hair, restrains his senses, sleeps on the ground, eats only barley scraps, cow dung, and cow urine, and donates cows constantly.

extraction_text: Yudhishthira shows great care for cows, praises them, stops using them for carts, and uses horses for travel instead.

attributes.details: He becomes diligent like a bull, avoids yoking cows, and switches to horses for long journeys.

extraction_text: Yudhishthira continues questioning Bhishma for more detailed explanations on cow donation.

attributes.details: Yudhishthira, still unsatisfied, asks Bhishma to elaborate more on the merits of cow donation.

extraction_text: King Yudhishthira (Dharma Raja) requested Bhishma (son of King Shantanu) to explain the merits of donating cows.

relationships: Bhishma is the grandsire and advisor to King Yudhishthira

extraction_text: Bhishma described the consequences of donating different types of cows to Brahmins.

attributes.details: Donating a healthy, young, cloth-covered cow with calf removes sins; donating a weak, non-milking cow leads to Asura world; donating an old, burden-carrying cow leads to dark hell; donating spoiled, sick, or unpaid-for cows brings no merit

extraction_text: Bhishma praised the Kapila cow as the best among cows, comparing it to the Ganga among rivers.
King Yudhishthira asked why cow donation (especially Kapila cow) is uniquely praised among all donations.
Bhishma explained he learned this from elders and began recounting the story related to creation by Daksha.
Lord Brahma commanded Daksha to create beings, and Daksha first created sustenance for them.
Daksha created food for beings, with animals highest among beings, humans highest among animals, and Brahmins highest among humans.
Soma (divine nectar) depends on sacrifices, sacrifices depend on Brahmins, and all are connected to cows.
Newly created beings cried for food and approached Daksha like children to a mother.
Daksha drank strengthening nectar, felt pleasure, belched, and vomited a fragrant substance that became the cow Surabhi.

supernatural_elements: Divine nectar consumption, miraculous creation from vomit

extraction_text: Surabhi gave birth to many daughters, golden-colored cows called Kapila, considered mothers of the world.
The cows sprayed milk that flowed in all directions, forming rivers with waves and foam produced from nectar.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Milk transforming into rivers with nectar properties

extraction_text: Calves suckled the milk, and some milk dripped from their mouths onto Shiva's head, angering the resting god.
Shiva looked up, and the eye in the middle of his forehead nearly burned the reddish-brown cows.
The powerful energy from Shiva's eye, like sun through clouds, changed the Kapila cows into various colors.
Some cows escaped to the moon god and retained their original color.
Daksha explained to Shiva that what fell on him was nectar, not impurity, comparing it to moon's pure light.
Daksha stated the cows would support all worlds with milk and offerings, and Shiva would enjoy the auspicious realm from nectar.
Daksha gave Shiva a bull and some cows, pleasing Rudra (Shiva).
Shiva made the bull his mount and emblem on his banner, earning the epithet 'One with the bull as banner'.
Gods consecrated him as 'Lord of Beasts' and 'One marked with the bull', making him master of cattle.
Kapila cows became the supreme object of charity, with great energy and unique colors, led by Rudra.
Cows are described as unparalleled, nourishing the world, born from flowing nectar, fulfilling wishes and giving life.
Reciting these verses about cows' birth with purity brings sons, cattle, wealth, and happiness, removing sins.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Mantra power for purification and prosperity

extraction_text: King Yudhishthira and his brothers listened to Bhishma's teachings about the merits of donating cows.

attributes.effect: Yudhishthira and his brothers became calm

extraction_text: Yudhishthira donated cows and golden milk buckets to excellent Brahmins.
Yudhishthira performed many sacrifices and donated hundreds of thousands of cows to Brahmins as payment for presiding over sacrifices.

attributes.purpose: To go to happy worlds in the afterlife and win good reputation
